062.name: Slavery in Brazil
062.hitokoto: The law that abolished slavery has only two articles.
body: Law No. 3,353 of 13 May 1888 has only two articles. Article 1: "From the date of this law, slavery is declared extinct in Brazil." Article 2: "All provisions to the contrary are repealed." It was assented to not by Emperor Pedro II but by Princess Isabel, who was then regent.

Those two articles took 38 years to reach. Law No. 581 of 4 September 1850 laid down "measures for the suppression of the African trade in this empire" and shut off the supply. Law No. 2,040 of 28 September 1871 declared that the children of slave women born after the date of the law were free, freeing those yet to be born before anyone else.

That it was done in stages is itself a sign that the institution was treated as part of the frame of the economy. The criterion that counts people as property left the law in 1888, twelve years before the 19th century ended. The past, when we call it the past, is not as far back as we assume.

made.label: Colonial era Slavery established
made.fact: Slavery in Brazil took shape in the colonial era. No primary source fixes a single year for its beginning, so the middle of the 16th century is given as an approximation. That the institution existed is shown by the text of the later abolition law, which takes it as given.

discontinued.label: 1888 The Golden Law
discontinued.fact: Law No. 3,353 of 13 May 1888, "declaring the extinction of slavery in Brazil". Article 1: "From the date of this law, slavery is declared extinct in Brazil." Article 2: "All provisions to the contrary are repealed." It was assented to by Princess Isabel as regent.

keyfacts.text: Law No. 3,353 of 13 May 1888 has only two articles. Article 1: "From the date of this law, slavery is declared extinct in Brazil." Article 2: "All provisions to the contrary are repealed."

It was assented to not by Emperor Pedro II but by Princess Isabel as regent (the signature reads "PRINCEZA IMPERIAL REGENTE"). The countersignature is that of Rodrigo Augusto da Silva, Minister of Agriculture, Commerce and Public Works.

Abolition did not come all at once. Law No. 581 of 4 September 1850 (the Eusébio de Queirós Law) laid down "measures for the suppression of the African trade in this empire" and stopped the import side.

Law No. 2,040 of 28 September 1871 (the Law of the Free Womb) declared that the children of slave women born after the date of the law were free, and freed the slaves held by the state. It was designed to free those yet to be born before anyone else.
From 1850 (the ban on the trade) to 1888 (the abolition of the institution) took 38 years. The date 1888 shows that slavery as an institution stood in the law until the end of the 19th century.

063.name: Execution as Spectacle
063.hitokoto: Three days after the last public hanging, the law that forbade them was passed.
body: The death penalty was something to be shown. The gallows went up in a town square or in front of a prison, crowds gathered, and the event served as an occasion for people to check the relation between crime and punishment with their own eyes. That the Act of 1868 had to order executions carried out "within the walls of the prison" is proof in itself that they had until then been public as a matter of course. The same Act also ordered the body buried within the prison grounds.

The last public hanging in Britain was on 26 May 1868. Michael Barrett, convicted over the Clerkenwell explosion, was executed in front of Newgate Prison. Three days later, on 29 May 1868, the Capital Punishment Amendment Act was assented to. The last crowd to watch a public execution and the law that forbade the practice fell in the same week.

What the Act abolished was not the death penalty but the showing of it. Its formal title is "An Act to provide for carrying out of Capital Punishment within Prisons". The first execution under the new arrangement took place on 13 August 1868 at Maidstone Prison, of Thomas Wells, aged 18. The hangman was William Calcraft, the same man as at the last public execution.

made.label: Early-modern Public hanging
made.fact: Executions were carried out in public, a spectacle that drew crowds. That the Act of 1868 had to order them carried out "within the walls of the prison" is itself a sign that they had been public as a matter of course. The same Act also ordered the body buried within the prison grounds.

discontinued.label: 29 May 1868 Executions moved inside prisons
discontinued.fact: The Capital Punishment Amendment Act 1868 (31 & 32 Vict. c. 24), assented to on 29 May 1868, bears the formal title "An Act to provide for carrying out of Capital Punishment within Prisons". It provided that everyone sentenced to death for murder be executed within the walls of the prison in which he was held, and that the body be buried within the prison grounds.

keyfacts.text: The Capital Punishment Amendment Act, assented to on 29 May 1868 (31 & 32 Vict. c. 24), ordered every execution carried out within the walls of the prison and the body buried within the prison grounds.
The last public hanging in Britain was on 26 May 1868, when the hangman William Calcraft executed Michael Barrett, a Fenian convicted over the Clerkenwell explosion, in front of Newgate Prison.
Only three days separate the last public execution (26 May) from the assent to the Act (29 May). The last crowd to watch a public execution and the law forbidding it fell in the same week.

The first private hanging under the Act was on 13 August 1868 at Maidstone Prison. Thomas Wells, 18, convicted of murdering Edward Walsh, the station master at Dover Priory, was executed by Calcraft again.
The formal title of the Act is "An Act to provide for carrying out of Capital Punishment within Prisons": its purpose was not to abolish the death penalty but to change where it was carried out.

064.name: Son Preference
064.hitokoto: Korea's sex ratio at birth was 116 in 1990. By 2024 it was back to 106.
body: The norm that the heir is a son has its roots in the patrilineal succession of the Joseon dynasty and in the idea of who carries out the ancestral rites. The house on the register passed from the head of household to male descendants in the direct line, and a daughter could not continue the line of the house. In a decision of 2005 the Constitutional Court defined the hoju system as "a system that constitutes the house as a notional collective body with the head of household at its apex, and passes it on through male descendants in the direct line".

When ultrasound diagnosis spread in the mid-1980s, the preference surfaced in the statistics as the sex ratio at birth. The number of boys per hundred girls rose from 106.1 in 1980 and reached its peak at 115.7 in 1990. In 1987 prenatal tests whose only purpose was to determine sex were forbidden, and in 1990 a doctor who had carried them out had his licence suspended. Heavier penalties together with the cost of the tests brought the ratio down from 1995 onward.

In 2007 it stood at 106.4, back inside the biologically normal range, and in 2024 it is 105.9. Over the same period the hoju system was abolished and a child could take the mother's surname and ancestral seat. China's sex ratio at birth has been falling since its peak of 117.8 in 2004, but at 110.3 in 2024 it has not returned to the normal range. As a case in which a preference disappeared from the statistics, Korea is cited again and again.

made.label: Joseon Patrilineal succession
made.fact: The norm that the heir is a son has its roots in the patrilineal succession of the Joseon dynasty and in the idea of who carries out the ancestral rites. The house on the register passed from the head of household to male descendants in the direct line, and a daughter could not continue the line of the house (Article 778 of the Civil Act, Act No. 471; the Constitutional Court's definition of the hoju system in case 2001 Hun-Ga 9). When ultrasound diagnosis spread in the mid-1980s, the preference surfaced in the statistics as the sex ratio at birth.

discontinued.label: 2007 Sex ratio back inside the normal range (106.4)
discontinued.fact: The number of boys per 100 girls peaked at 115.7 in 1990 and then fell year after year, reaching 106.4 in 2007, back inside the biologically normal range of 105 to 106. In 2024 it was 105.9. On the legal side, the hoju system of household heads was abolished on 1 January 2008, and a child could then take the mother's surname and ancestral seat.

keyfacts.text: The World Bank series for the sex ratio at birth (boys per 100 girls) shows Korea rising from 106.1 in 1980 to a peak of 115.7 in 1990. It then fell year after year, to 106.4 in 2007 and 105.9 in 2024.

In 1987 prenatal screening in Korea was limited to detecting genetic disease and monitoring growth, and tests whose only purpose was to determine sex were forbidden. In 1990 a doctor who had carried out such tests was arrested and his licence suspended. Heavier penalties together with the cost of the tests turned the sex ratio at birth downward from 1995.
Where there is no intervention, the biologically expected sex ratio at birth is put at 105 to 106 per 100. Korea's figure for 1990 was about ten points above that.

With the abolition of the hoju system on 1 January 2008, the legal frame that passed the house on through male descendants in the direct line was gone. The rule that a child took the father's surname and ancestral seat was also changed, and the mother's surname could be chosen.

In the same World Bank series, China's sex ratio at birth has been falling since its peak of 117.8 in 2004, but at 110.3 in 2024 it has not returned to the biologically normal range. Korea is the only country in East Asia of which it can be said that son preference has gone from the statistics.

Earlier work ties the weakening of the preference to modernisation and to the rise in women's social and economic standing. For Taiwan too, a decline in son preference and a rise in gender indifference since 1990 have been reported.

curve.title: Korea's sex ratio at birth ◆(boys per 100 girls)

065.name: Child labour as normal
065.hitokoto: A law was needed to forbid work under nine. So children under nine were working.
body: The Health and Morals of Apprentices Act 1802 limited the work of apprentices in cotton mills to 12 hours a day and forbade night work between 9 p.m. and 6 a.m. That 12 hours is written in as a "limit" tells you what the state of things had been. The Act also required ventilation windows, cleaning twice a year, and instruction in reading, writing and arithmetic during the first four years. That children worked at all was left as given.

The Cotton Mills Act 1819 forbade the employment of children under nine and limited those aged 9 to 16 to 12 hours a day. But a justice of the peace needed sworn evidence before he could enter a mill, and the Act barely moved. Articles without enforcement do not change what people value. The turn came with the Factory Act assented to on 29 August 1833 and in force from 1 January the following year.

The Act of 1833 forbade the employment of children under nine, limited those aged 9 to 13 to 8 hours a day and 48 hours a week, and those aged 14 to 18 to 12 hours a day. What was really new, though, was that it placed a professional Factory Inspectorate under the Home Office and gave it the power to enter without warning and the powers of a justice of the peace. The Mines and Collieries Act 1842 forbade women and children to work underground.

made.label: Late 18th century The factory standard
made.fact: The Health and Morals of Apprentices Act 1802 (42 Geo. 3 c. 73), brought in by Robert Peel, limited the work of apprentices in cotton mills to 12 hours a day, forbade night work between 9 p.m. and 6 a.m., and required ventilation windows, cleaning twice a year, and instruction in reading, writing and arithmetic during the first four years. That a limit had to be set by statute is itself a sign that there had been none before.

discontinued.label: 29 August 1833 The Factory Act (no work under nine)
discontinued.fact: The Labour of Children, etc., in Factories Act 1833 (3 & 4 Will. 4 c. 103, known as Althorp's Act), assented to on 29 August 1833 and in force from 1 January 1834, forbade the employment of children under nine (silk mills excepted), limited those aged 9 to 13 to 48 hours a week and 8 hours a day with an hour for dinner and those aged 14 to 18 to 12 hours a day with an hour for dinner, and forbade night work between 8.30 p.m. and 5.30 a.m. for anyone under 18. It also created a professional Factory Inspectorate under the Home Office, with the power to enter without warning and the powers of a justice of the peace.

keyfacts.text: The Health and Morals of Apprentices Act 1802 (42 Geo. 3 c. 73) limited apprentices in cotton mills to 12 hours a day and forbade night work between 9 p.m. and 6 a.m. The 12 hours is written in as a "limit".

The Cotton Mills Act 1819 (59 Geo. 3 c. 66) forbade the employment of children under nine and limited those aged 9 to 16 to 12 hours a day, but a justice of the peace needed sworn evidence to enter, and it had no real effect.

The Factory Act 1833 (3 & 4 Will. 4 c. 103) was assented to on 29 August 1833 and came into force on 1 January 1834. No employment under nine; 8 hours a day and 48 hours a week for those aged 9 to 13; 12 hours a day for those aged 14 to 18.

The decisive difference in the Act of 1833 was enforcement. For the first time in Britain it placed a professional Factory Inspectorate under the Home Office and gave it the power to enter without warning and to demand admission, the powers of a justice of the peace, and the power to make rules of enforcement independently of the Home Secretary.
The Mines and Collieries Act 1842 forbade women and children to work underground. It followed the campaign of Lord Ashley, later Earl of Shaftesbury, and the report of a royal commission.

066.name: Discipline by Force
066.hitokoto: Corporal punishment in schools was forbidden in 1879. By parents, in 2020.
body: Corporal punishment in schools was forbidden far earlier than people suppose. Article 46 of the Education Order, Grand Council Proclamation No. 40 of 29 September 1879: "In no school shall corporal punishment (striking or binding and the like) be inflicted on pupils." It is the 46th of 47 articles. Article 11 of the present School Education Act also states, in its proviso, that "corporal punishment may not be inflicted".

At home it went the other way. Article 882 of the Civil Code of 1898 provided that "a father or mother exercising parental authority may chastise the child himself within the necessary limits, or may place the child in a house of correction with the permission of the court". The power to strike the child yourself and the power to put the child in an institution with the court's permission stand side by side in the same article. The period was up to six months, fixed by the court.

The house of correction went with the amendment of 1947, but the right of chastisement remained. Corporal punishment by parents was forbidden in express words only on 1 April 2020, the day the amended Article 14 of the Act on the Prevention of Child Abuse came into force. The right of chastisement in Article 822 of the Civil Code was deleted, and Article 821, on respecting the personality of the child, put in its place, on 16 December 2022. That was 143 years after the ban in schools.

made.label: Pre-modern The patriarch's chastisement / 1898 Civil Code Article 882
made.fact: Article 882 of Act No. 9 of 1898 (Book 4 of the Civil Code, Relatives): "A father or mother exercising parental authority may chastise the child himself within the necessary limits, or may place the child in a house of correction with the permission of the court. The period for which a child is placed in a house of correction is fixed by the court within a limit of six months." The power of a parent to chastise the child himself, and the power to place the child in an institution with the court's permission, were both written into the article. A child was "subject to the parental authority of the father in his house" (Article 877), and where the mother exercised parental authority the consent of the family council was required (Article 886).

discontinued.label: 2022 Civil Code Article 822 deleted
discontinued.fact: The Act Partially Amending the Civil Code and Other Acts (Act No. 102 of 2022), promulgated and in force on 16 December 2022, deleted Article 822 of the Civil Code, which had provided for the right of chastisement. A new Article 821 was added at the same time: "A person exercising parental authority shall, in the custody and education provided for in the preceding Article, respect the personality of the child and have regard to the child's age and stage of development, and shall not use corporal punishment or any other words or conduct harmful to the sound development of the child in body or mind."

keyfacts.text: Corporal punishment in schools was already forbidden in 1879. Article 46 of the Education Order, Grand Council Proclamation No. 40 of 29 September 1879: "In no school shall corporal punishment (striking or binding and the like) be inflicted on pupils." The Education Order has 47 articles in all and was laid down on the abolition of the Education System Order.

Article 11 of the present School Education Act (Act No. 26 of 31 March 1947) provides that "the principal and teachers may, when they find it necessary for educational purposes, impose discipline on children, pupils and students as provided by the Minister of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology; provided, however, that corporal punishment may not be inflicted".

At home, Article 882 of the Meiji Civil Code provided for a parent's right of chastisement, and went further in giving the power to place a child in a "house of correction" with the permission of the court. The period was to be fixed by the court within a limit of six months.

Corporal punishment by parents was forbidden in express words in 2020. The Act Partially Amending the Child Welfare Act and Other Acts to Strengthen Measures for the Prevention of Child Abuse (Act No. 46 of 2019), promulgated on 26 June 2019, amended Article 14 of the Act on the Prevention of Child Abuse, and that amendment came into force on 1 April 2020.

Article 14, paragraph 1 of the amended Act on the Prevention of Child Abuse provides that "a person exercising parental authority over a child shall, in disciplining the child, respect the personality of the child and have regard to the child's age and stage of development, and shall not use corporal punishment or any other words or conduct harmful to the sound development of the child in body or mind".

The right of chastisement was deleted from the Civil Code on 16 December 2022, the same day Act No. 102 of 2022 was promulgated. Article 821 (respect for the personality of the child and the like) was added at the same time.

067.name: Castrato
067.hitokoto: One decree, dated 22 November 1903, gave the high voices of the church back to boys.
body: In 1589 a bull of Pope Sixtus V reorganised the choir of St Peter's on a footing that included castrati. The first castrati formally admitted to the Sistine Chapel were Folignato and Rosini, in 1599. Under an order in which women could not sing in church, the high voice became something made. The practice lasted 300 years.

The end came in stages. After the unification of Italy in 1861, the adoption of the penal code of the Kingdom of Sardinia made castration unlawful in the country. In 1878 Pope Leo XIII forbade the hiring of new castrati, but those already in post stayed on. The law of the state and the practice of the church thus stood side by side, out of step, for more than 40 years.

On 22 November 1903, the feast of St Cecilia, Pius X directed in the motu proprio Tra le sollecitudini that the high parts, soprano and alto, should be sung by boys, following the most ancient usage of the church. The last castrato of the Sistine Chapel, Alessandro Moreschi, left recordings made in 1902 and 1904 and retired in March 1913. Only the voice remains as physical evidence.

made.label: 1589 A papal bull takes in castrati
made.fact: In 1589 Pope Sixtus V, in the bull Cum pro nostro pastorali munere, reorganised the choir of St Peter's in Rome on a footing that included castrati. The first castrati formally admitted to the choir of the Sistine Chapel were Pietro Paolo Folignato and Girolamo Rosini, in 1599 (there are earlier cases of membership, such as Hernando Bustamante, who joined in 1558).

discontinued.label: 22 November 1903 Pius X's motu proprio
discontinued.fact: On 22 November 1903, the feast of St Cecilia, Pope Pius X directed in the motu proprio Tra le sollecitudini that the high parts, soprano and alto, must be sung by boys (fanciulli), "following the most ancient usage of the Church". This in effect ended the practice of castrati in the church. Pope Leo XIII had already forbidden the hiring of new castrati in 1878, but those in post remained in the Sistine Chapel and elsewhere.

keyfacts.text: In 1589 the bull Cum pro nostro pastorali munere of Pope Sixtus V reorganised the choir of St Peter's on a footing that included castrati.

After the unification of Italy in 1861, the adoption of the penal code of the Kingdom of Sardinia made castration unlawful in the country. The practice of the church and the law of the state stood side by side, out of step, for more than 40 years.
In 1878 Pope Leo XIII forbade the hiring of new castrati. Those already in post, however, remained in the Sistine Chapel and in the other papal basilicas.
The motu proprio Tra le sollecitudini of 22 November 1903 directed that the high parts, soprano and alto, be sung by boys. This was the decisive blow.

Alessandro Moreschi (1858-1922), the last castrato of the Sistine Chapel, is the only castrato to have left solo recordings; they were made in 1902 and 1904, and he retired in March 1913. The recordings straddle the year of the ban.

068.name: Kazoedoshi
068.hitokoto: To change how age is spoken the state made a statute. In force on 1 January 1950.
body: Under kazoedoshi, the year of birth is one and a year is added at each New Year's Day. In Japan before the modern period this was the only way of counting, and shichi-go-san, the unlucky years and the celebrations of old age were all built on it. Age reckoned from birth became law with the Act on Calculation of Ages (Act No. 50 of 1902), promulgated on 2 December 1902. The rule of calculation had changed at the beginning of the 20th century.

Everyday speech, however, did not change. Forty-seven years later the state made a statute about the manner of speaking itself: the Act on How Ages Are Stated (Act No. 96 of 1949), promulgated on 24 May 1949. Paragraph 1 wrote that people should "change the customary practice of stating age by kazoedoshi" and "endeavour to make it the rule" to state it by age reckoned from birth.

For the public it is a duty to make the effort. The duty proper fell on the organs of the state and of local government, which, where they had no choice but to use kazoedoshi, had to "state expressly that they are doing so". The supplementary provisions ordered the government to "give particularly active guidance". The day of entry into force was 1 January 1950: the counting changed on the day that adds a year.

made.label: Pre-modern (the year of birth counts as one)
made.fact: The East Asian way of counting age in which the year of birth is one and a year is added at each New Year's Day. In Japan before the modern period it was the only way of counting, and the rites of passage, shichi-go-san, the unlucky years and the celebrations of old age, were built on it. Age reckoned from birth was put into law in 1902, and even after that kazoedoshi went on being used as the everyday way of counting.

discontinued.label: 1950 A statute on how age is stated
discontinued.fact: The Act on How Ages Are Stated (Act No. 96), promulgated on 24 May 1949. Under paragraph 1 of its supplementary provisions it came into force on 1 January 1950. Paragraph 1 provided that "from the day this Act comes into force, the people shall change the customary practice of stating age by kazoedoshi and endeavour to make it the rule to state it by the number of years, or where it is less than one year the number of months, calculated under the provisions of the Act on Calculation of Ages (Act No. 50 of 1902)".

keyfacts.text: Age reckoned from birth had been law since 1902: the Act on Calculation of Ages (Act No. 50 of 2 December 1902, in force 22 December 1902). Because the everyday way of counting still did not shift from kazoedoshi, a statute on the manner of speaking itself was needed 47 years later.

The Act on How Ages Are Stated (Act No. 96 of 24 May 1949) runs to two paragraphs and two supplementary provisions, and as regards the public it went no further than a duty to endeavour, to "make the effort".

On public bodies it laid a duty. Paragraph 2: "From the day this Act comes into force, where an organ of the state or of a local public entity states an age, that organ shall state it by the number of years or months provided for in the preceding paragraph. Provided that where, for reasons that are particularly unavoidable, it states an age by kazoedoshi, it shall state expressly that it is doing so."

Paragraph 2 of the supplementary provisions laid a duty on the government too: "The government shall give particularly active guidance so that the people generally understand the purport of this Act and observe it." That the state would guide people in changing how they count was written into the statute.

The day of entry into force was set at 1 January 1950, more than half a year after promulgation in 1949 (supplementary provisions, paragraph 1: "This Act shall come into force from 1 January 1950"). It answers to the fact that kazoedoshi added a year at the turn of the year.

069.name: Smacking Children
069.hitokoto: The first country to forbid smacking a child at home was Sweden, on 1 July 1979.
body: That parents and teachers hit children was not merely custom; it had the law behind it. In Sweden that backing was taken away piece by piece. Corporal punishment in schools was forbidden in the gymnasium in 1918, in the state secondary schools in 1928, and in all schools in 1958. The parental right of chastisement was struck from the criminal law in 1957, and the provision in the Children and Parents Code in 1966.

On 1 July 1979 Sweden brought into force an amendment to the Children and Parents Code. "A child is entitled to care, security and a good upbringing. A child is to be treated with respect for its person and individuality and may not be subjected to corporal punishment or other humiliating treatment." It is the first law in the world to forbid corporal punishment outright, inside the home included. The present text was placed in chapter 6, section 1 by the amendment of 1983.

Finland followed in 1984, Norway in 1987 and Austria in 1989, and as of 2021, 22 of the 27 EU states have a ban. Britain is late. Corporal punishment in state schools was forbidden in 1986; at home, Scotland abolished the defence of "reasonable chastisement" by an Act of 2019, and Wales followed in 2020. In England that defence still stands.

made.label: Pre-modern The right to chastise
made.fact: The right of parents and teachers to hit a child was backed not only by custom but by law. In Sweden corporal punishment in schools was forbidden step by step (the gymnasium in 1918, the state secondary schools in 1928, all schools in 1958), the parental right of chastisement was struck from the criminal law in 1957, and the provision in the Children and Parents Code (föräldrabalken) in 1966. The full ban of 1979 is the last stroke in that long paring away.

discontinued.label: 1 July 1979 A full ban, the home included (the first)
discontinued.fact: On 1 July 1979 Sweden brought into force an amendment to the Children and Parents Code (Föräldrabalken): "A child is entitled to care, security and a good upbringing. A child is to be treated with respect for its person and individuality and may not be subjected to corporal punishment or other humiliating treatment." It is the first country in the world to write into law a full ban on corporal punishment, the home included. The present provision stands in chapter 6, section 1 of the Code, from the amendment of 1983 (Lag 1983:47).

keyfacts.text: On 1 July 1979 Sweden became the first country in the world to forbid corporal punishment of children outright, the home included.

The present text of chapter 6, section 1 of the Children and Parents Code reads "Barn skall behandlas med aktning för sin person och egenart och får inte utsättas för kroppslig bestraffning eller annan kränkande behandling". This section number and wording come from the amendment of 1983 (Lag 1983:47) and are not the text of 1979 itself.
The Swedish ban on corporal punishment in schools came in stages: the gymnasium in 1918, the state secondary schools in 1928, all schools including the folkskola in 1958.
The first country in the world to forbid corporal punishment in schools was Poland, in 1783, 175 years before Sweden's 1958.

The countries that followed Sweden: Finland 1984, Norway 1987, Austria 1989, Cyprus 1994, Denmark and Poland 1997, Latvia 1998, Croatia 1999, Bulgaria, Israel and Germany 2000, Iceland 2003, Ukraine and Romania 2004. As of 2021, 22 of the 27 EU states have a ban.

In Britain the Education (No. 2) Act 1986 forbade corporal punishment in state schools (passed by Parliament on 22 July 1986); private schools were covered in England in 1998, in Scotland in 2000 and in Northern Ireland in 2003. As to the home, Scotland abolished the defence of "reasonable chastisement" by the Children (Equal Protection from Assault) (Scotland) Act 2019 (2019 asp 16), which under section 4 came into force 12 months after it was passed. Wales also passed an Act abolishing the same defence in 2020, but in England corporal punishment in the home has still not been made unlawful.

070.name: Bound by Indenture
070.hitokoto: The article that repealed this proclamation is still in the statute book.
body: On the second day of the tenth month of 1872, Grand Council Proclamation No. 295 was issued. Its title runs "Forbidding the Sale of Persons, Fixing the Terms of Servants, Freeing Performers and Prostitutes, and Refusing to Hear Suits over Loans in Connection Therewith". Paragraph 1 states that although the sale of persons "has long been forbidden", it had gone on "under various names such as service for a term of years", and that it was strictly forbidden from now on. The government is writing down, itself, that its own prohibition had not been kept.

What told was not the words of the ban but paragraph 4: "Prostitutes, performers and all indentured servants are to be set free, and no suit over loans in connection therewith is to be taken up." One line saying the courts would not hear claims for money advanced. Paragraph 2 set apprenticeship at not more than seven full years and paragraph 3 ordinary servants at one year at a time: service itself was left standing, and separated from sale by putting a term on it.

When the proclamation was repealed can also be followed in the articles. Article 9 of the Act on Enforcement of the Civil Code reads "The following laws are repealed from the day the Civil Code comes into force: 1. Proclamation No. 295 of 1872". The day the Civil Code came into force is 16 July 1898. The Act on Enforcement of the Civil Code is still a law in force, so that line remains in the collection of laws now in force. A statutory frame for punishing prostitution comes only later, with the Anti-Prostitution Act promulgated on 24 May 1956.

made.label: Early-modern Indentured service
made.fact: All through early-modern times an arrangement was widespread under the name nenki-boko, service for a term of years: a person was handed over, for life or for a fixed term, and made to work against money advanced. Grand Council Proclamation No. 295 of 1872 states that the sale of persons "has long been forbidden, yet under various names such as service for a term of years people have been placed in service, and the practice has come in truth to be the same as sale". The government is acknowledging, in its own words, that the prohibition had gone on being ignored under the name of service.

discontinued.label: 1872 Grand Council Proclamation No. 295
discontinued.fact: Grand Council Proclamation No. 295 of the second day of the tenth month of 1872, "Forbidding the Sale of Persons, Fixing the Terms of Servants, Freeing Performers and Prostitutes, and Refusing to Hear Suits over Loans in Connection Therewith". It made the sale of persons "strictly forbidden from now on", set the term of apprenticeship at not more than seven full years and that of ordinary servants at one year at a time, and provided that "prostitutes, performers and all indentured servants are to be set free, and no suit over loans in connection therewith is to be taken up", so that the courts were not to entertain claims over money advanced. The proclamation itself was repealed on the day the Civil Code came into force, 16 July 1898, under Article 9, item 1 of the Act on Enforcement of the Civil Code (Act No. 11 of 1898).

keyfacts.text: Paragraph 1 of Proclamation No. 295: "To sell a person, and for life or for a term of years to use them harshly at the master's pleasure, is against human decency and is not a thing that should be; it has long been forbidden, yet under various names such as service for a term of years people have been placed in service, and the practice has come in truth to be the same as sale, which is beyond all expectation; from now on it shall be strictly forbidden."

Paragraph 4: "Prostitutes, performers and all indentured servants are to be set free, and no suit over loans in connection therewith is to be taken up." Alongside the ban, a measure was taken that put the recovery of money advanced outside the courts. It is this refusal to hear such suits that was later called the "cutting loose of cattle and horses".

Paragraph 2: "Placing a child in apprenticeship to learn a trade in farming, manufacture or commerce is at the parties' discretion, but the term must not exceed seven full years." Paragraph 3: "Ordinary servants shall be engaged one year at a time." Service itself was not forbidden; it was separated from sale by putting a term on it.

The base text of the proclamation is Horei zensho, the complete collection of laws, for 1872 (Cabinet Bureau of Official Gazettes). The original can be read at frame 157 of the National Diet Library Digital Collections.

Article 9 of the Act on Enforcement of the Civil Code (Act No. 11 of 1898): "The following laws are repealed from the day the Civil Code comes into force: 1. Proclamation No. 295 of 1872..." The proclamation was repealed on 16 July 1898. The Act on Enforcement of the Civil Code is still a law in force and still printed in the collection of laws in force.

The Anti-Prostitution Act (Act No. 118 of 1956) was promulgated on 24 May 1956. Under paragraph 1 of its supplementary provisions, "This Act shall come into force from 1 April 1957, provided that Chapter 2 and paragraph 2 of the supplementary provisions shall come into force from 1 April 1958", the penal provisions took effect from 1 April 1958.

Paragraph 2 of the same supplementary provisions: "The Imperial Ordinance on the Punishment of Persons Who Cause Women to Engage in Prostitution and Others (Imperial Ordinance No. 9 of 1947) is repealed." That an imperial ordinance promulgated and in force on 15 January 1947 had bridged the years up to the Anti-Prostitution Act is recorded in those supplementary provisions.

A week after the proclamation, on the ninth day of the tenth month of 1872, the Ministry of Justice issued Instruction No. 22, "Disposal of Loans to Prostitutes and Performers and Other Practices Akin to the Sale of Persons". Its Article 2 reads: "Such prostitutes and performers are persons who have lost the rights of a person and are no different from cattle or horses; there is no reason for a person to demand repayment of anything from cattle or horses; therefore no money lent to such prostitutes and performers, nor any unpaid account, may be recovered at all." It is this passage that gave the instruction its popular name, the "cattle-and-horse cutting-loose order".

Article 1 of the same instruction treated the capital advanced for the hire as "stolen money" and had it taken away in full, and Article 3 provided that making a girl a prostitute or performer under the name of an adopted daughter was in substance the sale of a person and was to be dealt with severely.

Shortly before the proclamation, in 1872, came the case of the Peruvian ship Maria Luz. She entered Yokohama on 5 June carrying 231 Chinese coolies, and judgment was given on 27 July on terms that freed the Chinese. The National Archives hold "A Brief Account of the Reasons for Trying the Peruvian Slave Ship That Entered Yokohama", dated the 23rd day of the ninth month of 1872. There is, however, a counter-argument as to the causal link with the emancipation order, namely that the matter had been under consideration within the government from the previous year.

Institutionalisation came after the ban. The Regulations for the Control of Prostitutes (Home Ministry Ordinance No. 44 of 2 October 1900, 15 articles) provided in Article 4, paragraph 2 that "the striking of a name from the register of prostitutes shall be applied for by the prostitute herself", and in Article 6 that "no person whatsoever may obstruct an application to strike a name from the register of prostitutes". The words "free cessation" appear nowhere in the text, and Article 7 restricted where a prostitute might live and made going out subject to permission: as a whole the regulations were not a liberalisation but the institution of police supervision.

The Regulations for the Control of Prostitutes were repealed on 2 February 1946 by Home Ministry Ordinance No. 3. The GHQ memorandum "Abolition of Licensed Prostitution in Japan" had been issued the previous month, on 21 January 1946, and the Police Bureau of the Home Ministry's "Inquiry concerning the Repeal of the Regulations for the Control of Prostitutes", drafted on 25 January, survives in the National Archives.

071.name: Seppuku
071.hitokoto: Seppuku stood in the penal code of the state for less than three years.
body: Seppuku is known as the honourable death of the samurai. Yet no article of shogunal law providing that "the death penalty for those of samurai standing is seppuku" can be found. The Kujikata osadamegaki, completed in 1742, was a strictly secret document, endorsed "none but the magistrates may see this". The findings of research grant 20K13306 state that the received idea that a heavy crime meant seppuku as a matter of course "does not necessarily correspond to the facts".

Self-execution appears as an article of law only after the Meiji Restoration. The Provisional Penal Code of 1868 set "the two degrees of beheading and self-stabbing" for those of samurai standing and above who committed a capital crime, and the New Code of the 20th day of the twelfth month of Meiji 3 ranked the penalties for samurai, from the lightest, as confinement at home, gate shut, imprisonment, frontier garrison duty and self-execution, writing that "one who merits death shall be put to self-execution". The first penal code of the modern state, that is, set out seppuku as a punishment.

It went on 13 June 1873, with the Revised Statutes, Grand Council Proclamation No. 206. Article 13 of the "revised law of supplementary penalties" provided that "the law putting him to confinement at home, gate shut, imprisonment, frontier garrison duty or self-execution is altered, and he shall in all cases be imprisoned". Sentences of self-execution handed down by a court are traced as far as the twelve former retainers of the Honda house of Kaga in the eleventh month of 1872. Yukio Mishima's suicide on 25 November 1970 falls 97 years after the article was gone.

made.label: 1868 Provisional Penal Code / 1870 The New Code
made.fact: Commuting the death penalty for those of samurai standing to self-execution (seppuku) became an article of law only after the Meiji Restoration. The Provisional Penal Code of 1868 provided that "for those of the imperial house and of the domains of samurai standing and above who commit a capital crime, the two degrees of beheading and self-stabbing shall serve as the concealed penalty", and the New Code (Shinritsu koryo), promulgated on the 20th day of the twelfth month of Meiji 3 (9 February 1871) as Grand Council No. 944 of Meiji 3, provided in the section on supplementary penalties in the General Rules: "Where a samurai commits an offence, if the principal offence merits the light cane he shall be confined at home; if the staff, his gate shall be shut; if penal servitude, he shall be imprisoned; if banishment, sent to a frontier post; if death, put to self-execution."

discontinued.label: 1873 The Revised Statutes, Article 13
discontinued.fact: Article 13 of the "revised law of supplementary penalties" in the Revised Statutes (Kaitei ritsurei, Grand Council Proclamation No. 206 of 13 June 1873) provided that "where a samurai commits an offence, the law putting him to confinement at home, gate shut, imprisonment, frontier garrison duty or self-execution is altered, and he shall in all cases be imprisoned". Self-execution was struck out and everything brought under imprisonment. Grand Council Proclamation No. 69 of 24 June 1874 then changed kinko imprisonment to kingoku, Grand Council Proclamation No. 76 of 2 November 1877 deleted the law of supplementary penalties itself, and the old Penal Code of 1880 abolished the supplementary penalties that treated samurai and officials specially.

keyfacts.text: The New Code was promulgated on the 20th day of the twelfth month of Meiji 3 (9 February 1871) as Grand Council No. 944 of Meiji 3. The section on supplementary penalties in the General Rules reads "Where a samurai commits an offence, if the principal offence merits the light cane he shall be confined at home; if the staff, his gate shall be shut; if penal servitude, he shall be imprisoned; if banishment, sent to a frontier post; if death, put to self-execution", so that the supplementary penalties for samurai run, from the lightest, in five degrees: confinement at home, gate shut, imprisonment, frontier garrison duty, self-execution.

Article 13 of the "revised law of supplementary penalties" in the Revised Statutes (Grand Council Proclamation No. 206 of 13 June 1873) provided that "where a samurai commits an offence, the law putting him to confinement at home, gate shut, imprisonment, frontier garrison duty or self-execution is altered, and he shall in all cases be imprisoned". The word self-execution leaves the statute book here.

There were rules of practice as well. On the seventh day of the fourth month of Meiji 4 the Secretariat of the Grand Council laid down the [Rules on Self-Execution] in answer to an inquiry from Kyoto Prefecture (the original is titled "Questions on the General Rules and the Rules on Self-Execution", Daijo ruiten, series 1, vol. 189, no. 22).

On the Edo side it is the received idea that is in doubt. The Kujikata osadamegaki (completed 1742) is a strictly secret document endorsed "none but the magistrates may see this", and no article providing that "the death penalty for those of samurai standing is seppuku" can be found in it. The findings of Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research 20K13306 (Svetlana Korneeva) state that "the idea current today, that for a man of samurai standing the punishment for a heavy crime such as killing was seppuku as a matter of course, does not necessarily correspond to the facts".

The tidying up went on after the Revised Statutes. Grand Council Proclamation No. 69 of 24 June 1874, "Changing kinko to kingoku in the Revised Law of Supplementary Penalties", and Grand Council Proclamation No. 76 of 2 November 1877, "Deleting and Amending the Law of Supplementary Penalties, the Law on Flight, the Rules on Redemption for the Old, the Young and the Disabled and Others in the Revised Statutes", which deleted the law of supplementary penalties itself; the old Penal Code of 1880 abolished the supplementary penalties for samurai and officials.

The last sentence of seppuku in Japanese legal history arises from a revenge case among the former retainers of the Honda house of Kaga. Masachika Honda, chief minister of the Kanazawa domain, was assassinated on the seventh day of the eighth month of 1869; his former retainers took their revenge and then gave themselves up, and in the eleventh month of 1872 twelve of them were ordered by the court to self-execute (the rest received from three to ten years' imprisonment). It is a case of the samurai supplementary penalties of the New Code being applied. The date is given as 4 November 1872.

There are two cases of seppuku before foreigners just after the Meiji government came in. Zenzaburo Taki of the Kobe incident cut himself open at Eifuku-ji in Kobe on the ninth day of the second month of Keio 4 (2 March 1868), with seven foreign witnesses present. In the Sakai incident, eleven samurai of the Tosa domain cut themselves open at Myokoku-ji in Sakai on the 23rd day of the second month of Keio 4 (16 March 1868). Both fall in 1868, not 1869.
Yukio Mishima's suicide on 25 November 1970 comes 97 years after seppuku as a punishment left the statute book. Seppuku as an institution and seppuku as a form have to be kept apart.

072.name: Blackened Teeth
072.hitokoto: It forbade not the women of the imperial family but those of the peerage coming of age.
body: Dyeing the teeth black with kane and plucking the eyebrows were, to begin with, rites of coming of age. On the account given by the National Diet Library, the first blackening was done at eight or nine in the Muromachi period; in the Edo period the age rose, and it was called "thirteen kane" or "seventeen kane", until in time it came to be done to coincide with the wedding. Eyebrow-plucking too moved to the time of marriage or childbirth. Down to medieval times men of the court and of the warrior houses dyed their teeth as well.

It came off from the men's side first. On the sixth day of the first month of Meiji 1, "The Dyeing of Teeth and the Drawing of Eyebrows by Young Men Is Left to Their Own Wishes" was issued and the sons of the court nobles were free; on the 19th of the same month came a notice warning against the "fashion for soft eyebrows" at court. On the first day of the third month of Meiji 2 the "wiping of the eyebrows" was performed at court. Then, on the fifth day of the second month of Meiji 3, the Grand Council issued "Stopping the Dyeing of Teeth and Sweeping of Eyebrows by Those of the Peerage Coming of Age". It applies to those of the peerage who are about to come of age.

The date on which Empress Dowager Shoken gave the practice up is often written as 3 March 1873, but the Index of Japanese Laws (Early Meiji) holds no proclamation or notice of 3 March 1873 to that effect, and 2 March is also given. Nor did the practice go as the notice said. A survey by a dentist in Wakayama Prefecture found that among those who came to his surgery in 1892, 274 of the 385 married women who still had teeth were blackening them. The date in the statute book and the end of the habit in front of the mirror are more than 20 years apart.

made.label: Early-modern A mark of coming of age and of marriage
made.fact: Dyeing the teeth black with kane and plucking or shaving the eyebrows were, to begin with, rites of coming of age. On the account given by the National Diet Library, the first blackening was done at eight or nine in the Muromachi period but came later in the Edo period, when it was called "thirteen kane", "seventeen kane" or "eighteen kane" and was most often done at 13, or at 17 or 18, until in time it "came in the Edo period to be done to coincide with the wedding". Eyebrow-plucking too "was originally a rite of coming of age, but came to be done at the time of marriage, pregnancy or childbirth". Down to medieval times men of the court and of the warrior houses also blackened their teeth, but the practice did not spread to commoner men in the Edo period.

discontinued.label: 1870 The peerage told to stop
discontinued.fact: On the fifth day of the second month of Meiji 3 the Grand Council issued a notice, "Stopping the Dyeing of Teeth and Sweeping of Eyebrows by Those of the Peerage Coming of Age". It is item 88 in Horei zensho for Meiji 3, and in the Index of Japanese Laws (Early Meiji) it is classed under "justice - civil matters - household and status registers - the status of the peerage and former samurai generally". It applies to those of the peerage "coming of age", that is, those about to do so. Before it, on the sixth day of the first month of Meiji 1, "The Dyeing of Teeth and the Drawing of Eyebrows by Young Men Is Left to Their Own Wishes" had been issued, leaving the dyeing of teeth and drawing of eyebrows by the sons of the court nobles free.

keyfacts.text: The notice of the Grand Council of the fifth day of the second month of Meiji 3 is titled "Stopping the Dyeing of Teeth and Sweeping of Eyebrows by Those of the Peerage Coming of Age". The number "Grand Council Proclamation No. 88", often given, is not a number at all: in the form column of the Index of Japanese Laws it is a "(notice)" without a number, and 88 is its item number in Horei zensho for Meiji 3.

It applies to the peerage; the imperial family is not included. Nor is it a provision limited to women: "those coming of age" means those about to do so. The title "Forbidding the Women of the Peerage to Blacken Their Teeth and Remove Their Eyebrows" does not exist in the Index of Japanese Laws.

Two things came before it: "The Dyeing of Teeth and the Drawing of Eyebrows by Young Men Is Left to Their Own Wishes" of the sixth day of the first month of Meiji 1 (item 9 in Horei zensho for Meiji 1), and "Warning the Courtiers and Officials to Study Both Letters and Arms and Not to Follow the Fashion for Soft Eyebrows" of the 19th day of the same month (Daijo ruiten, series 1, vol. 6, no. 30). It came off from the men's side first.

On the 22nd day of the second month of Meiji 2 the Executive Office issued "On the Wiping of the Eyebrows on the First of Next Month, the Courtiers Are to Attend and Offer Congratulations" (item 182 in Horei zensho for Meiji 2). It records that the "wiping of the eyebrows" was performed at court on the first day of the third month of Meiji 2 and that the courtiers were made to attend.

No primary source could be reached for the claim that "Empress Dowager Shoken gave up blackened teeth and plucked eyebrows on 3 March 1873". The Index of Japanese Laws (Early Meiji) holds no proclamation or notice dated 3 March 1873 on teeth or eyebrows; the Japan Dental Association gives 3 March and HITNET, at the National Museum of Nature and Science, gives 2 March, while several museums and research bodies go no closer than "March 1873".

The practice outlived the notice for some time. Yoshimasa Nakamura, a dentist in practice in Wakayama Prefecture, reported in Shika kenkyukai geppo, no. 39 (published March 1894) on a survey over the eight months from May to December 1892: of the 589 women who came to his surgery, 274 of the 385 married women who still had teeth, rather more than 70%, were blackening them.

There is no agreement on when it died out. The Japan Dental Association holds that it took about half a century to fade, saying that "even in the early years of the Second World War one might still come upon the sight of blackened teeth in country districts", while HITNET puts it at "about the end of the Meiji era". No firm answer is possible.

In the same years, the regulation of how the body looked reached women's hair as well. Tokyo Prefecture Notice No. 32 of 5 April 1872 forbade women to cut their hair short, and the prefecture's inquiry to the Grand Council, "Inquiry concerning Women Cutting Their Hair", survives in Kobunroku. The Tokyo Misdemeanour Regulations of 8 November the same year (in force from the 13th, 48 articles) also have a provision on "those who cut their hair short".

073.name: Sati (widow immolation)
073.hitokoto: Widow burning, held to be a virtue, became a criminal offence on 4 December 1829.
body: The authorities in British India counted, presidency by presidency, the cases in which a widow was burned with her husband's body. A report of April 1829 gives 5,997 cases over ten years in the Bengal Presidency, about 600 a year; over the same ten years the Madras and Bombay Presidencies together give 635. How exact the counts were is disputed, but that the administration was counting at all shows that this was not a series of separate incidents but an institution.

On 4 December 1829 the Governor-General, William Bentinck, with his council, issued Regulation XVII. Its title: a regulation declaring the practice of burning or burying alive the widows of Hindus illegal and punishable by the criminal courts. An act that had been praised became a criminal offence by one regulation with a date on it. It spread to the princely states as well; Kolhapur proclaimed a ban in 1841.

158 years later, on 4 September 1987, came the case of an 18-year-old woman at Deorala in Rajasthan. The state issued an ordinance on 1 October, and Parliament passed the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act 1987, assented to on 3 January 1988. What this Act newly punished was not the act itself but its glorification: processions, temples and even trusts came within it. The law names, a second time, what is left after a ban.

made.label: Pre-modern (a practice recorded in the early 19th century)
made.fact: A report of April 1829 gives 5,997 cases of burning or burying alive in the Bengal Presidency over ten years, an average of about 600 a year, and 635 cases in the Madras and Bombay Presidencies together over the same ten years. The figures are open to argument, but that the authorities were counting the cases at all shows that the practice existed as an institution.

discontinued.label: 1829 Bengal Regulation XVII
discontinued.fact: On 4 December 1829 the Governor-General, William Bentinck, with his council, issued Regulation XVII of 1829 in the Bengal Code. Its formal title is "A Regulation for declaring the practice of Sati or of Burning or Burying alive the Widows of Hindus, illegal, and punishable by the Criminal Courts", declaring it liable to punishment in the criminal courts.

keyfacts.text: On 4 December 1829 the Governor-General of Bengal, William Bentinck, with his council, issued Regulation XVII, declaring sati illegal and punishable by the criminal courts.

The formal title of the regulation is "A Regulation for declaring the practice of Sati or of Burning or Burying alive the Widows of Hindus, illegal, and punishable by the Criminal Courts", and it was compiled as Regulation XVII of 1829 in the Bengal Code.
A report of April 1829 records 5,997 cases over ten years in the Bengal Presidency (an average of about 600 a year) and 635 in the Madras and Bombay Presidencies together over the same period.
It spread to the princely states as well: Kolhapur issued a proclamation of prohibition in 1841.
On 4 September 1987 the case of Roop Kanwar, aged 18, occurred at Deorala in Sikar district, Rajasthan, and on 1 October that year Rajasthan issued its Sati Prevention Ordinance.

The Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act 1987 received the President's assent on 3 January 1988 and became Act No. 3 of 1988. Its preamble states that "sati, that is, the burning or burying alive of widows or women, is revolting to the feelings of human nature and is nowhere enjoined by any of the religions of India as an imperative duty", and section 2(1)(c) defines it as such "whether such burning or burying is claimed to be voluntary or otherwise". Under section 1(3) the day of commencement is fixed state by state by notification in the official gazette, so the Act has no single nationwide commencement date.

074.name: Widows must not remarry
074.hitokoto: The 1856 Act that let widows remarry also took away their inheritance if they did.
body: A woman who had lost her husband was held to owe the rest of her life to abstinence, and remarriage was treated as religiously void. So the Act of 1856 had first to write that a remarriage was valid and that the children born of it were not to be held illegitimate. The strength of a norm shows in how plain the provision has to be that cancels it.

The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act was enacted as Act XV of 1856 on 26 July that year. Governor-General Dalhousie put the bill into its final form himself, and it became law under Governor-General Canning. Vidyasagar petitioned the Legislative Council, but the counter-petition of the Dharma Sabha carried nearly four times as many signatures. There were numbers on the other side too.

Section 2 of the same Act, however, provided that a widow's rights in her late husband's property should cease on remarriage "as if she had then died". Remarriage was allowed in exchange for taking the inheritance away. Because of that section, the Act itself was struck out by a repealing Act of 1983. A tool of emancipation was disposed of 127 years later as a discriminatory provision.

made.label: Pre-modern (the norm of the ascetic widow)
made.fact: A woman who had lost her husband was held to owe the rest of her life to abstinence and self-denial, and remarriage was treated as religiously void. It was against that norm that the Act of 1856 had to declare that a remarriage was valid and that the children born of it were not to be held illegitimate.

discontinued.label: 1856 Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (Act XV of 1856)
discontinued.fact: Enacted on 26 July 1856. It made the remarriage of widows lawful throughout the jurisdictions under East India Company rule. Governor-General Dalhousie drafted the bill and it became law under Governor-General Canning. Section 1 made remarriage valid and recognised the legitimacy of the children.

keyfacts.text: The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (Act XV of 1856) was enacted on 26 July 1856. It made the remarriage of widows lawful throughout the jurisdictions under East India Company rule and provided that the children of such a marriage were not to be held illegitimate.

Governor-General Dalhousie put the bill into its final form himself, and it became law under Governor-General Canning. Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar petitioned the Legislative Council, but the counter-petition of Radhakanta Deb and the Dharma Sabha carried nearly four times as many signatures.

Section 2 of the Act provided that "all rights and interests which a widow may have in her deceased husband's property shall, upon her remarriage, cease as if she had then died". An Act that allowed remarriage carried at the same time a provision taking the inheritance from those who remarried.
Because of that section 2, the Act was repealed 127 years later by the Hindu Widows' Remarriage (Repeal) Act 1983. A law made for emancipation was in the end struck out as a discriminatory provision.

Japan has a corresponding institution. From the Meiji Civil Code onward a period during which remarriage was forbidden was imposed on women alone; it was cut from six months to 100 days in 2016, and abolished by the amendment to the Civil Code of 2022, in force on 1 April 2024. In Turkey too, Article 95 of the Civil Code of 1926 imposed a waiting period of 300 days on widows and divorced women.
